---
title: Blog template
---

The group has a [Quarto](https://quarto.org) template for a blog of research
notes in the [blog-template](https://github.com/tolborg-group/blog-template)
repository. A blog can be a log for a single project or one place for all of
your work: short write-ups of results, convergence tests, notes on a method,
or the figures for the next group meeting. Posts are written in Markdown, can
run Python to make their figures and tables from the data, and support
equations, citations and cross-references in the same way as a paper.

Like the [paper template](paper-template.qmd), the blog uses [Pixi](pixi.qmd)
to install everything it needs, so the only prerequisite is that Pixi is
installed. The rendered example blog can be seen at
<https://tolborg-group.github.io/blog-template/>, and its example posts are the
best introduction to writing posts. The
[README](https://github.com/tolborg-group/blog-template#readme) of the
repository is the reference for the details.

## Published or local?

Before starting, decide whether the blog should be public:

Published
: The repository is public, and GitHub Pages publishes the blog as a website
  that anyone can read. Every push to `main` updates the website.

Local
: The repository is private, or not on GitHub at all, and the blog is only
  viewed on your own machine with `pixi run preview`. This works fine for
  showing the blog at a group meeting.

::: {.callout-warning}
A site published by GitHub Pages is public even when the repository is
private. Use the local setup for unpublished results and anything else that
should not be public.
:::

## Starting a blog

The repository is a GitHub template, so a new blog is made with **Use this
template** on its GitHub page, or with the [GitHub CLI](https://cli.github.com):

```bash
gh repo create tolborg-group/my-blog --template tolborg-group/blog-template --public --clone
cd my-blog
```

using `--private` instead of `--public` for a local blog. Then

1. *Published:* on GitHub, go to **Settings → Pages** of the new repository
   and set **Source** to **GitHub Actions**. The blog is then published at
   `https://tolborg-group.github.io/my-blog/`.

   *Local:* delete `.github/workflows/publish.yml`. Otherwise GitHub tries to
   publish the blog on every push, and the run fails.
2. In `_quarto.yml`, change `title`, `site-url` and the GitHub link in the
   navigation bar to point to your blog.
3. Rewrite `about.qmd` to describe what the blog is for.
4. Once you have read the example posts, delete them and their stored results,
   as described in the README.

## Previewing

```bash
pixi run preview
```

renders the blog and opens it in the browser, and updates the page whenever a
file is saved. `pixi run render` renders the whole blog into `_site/` without
opening it.

## Writing a post

Each post is a folder in `posts/` with an `index.qmd` file in it:

```
posts/2026-11-20-phonon-results/
├── index.qmd
├── references.bib
└── phonons.csv
```

Starting the folder name with the date keeps the posts in order. Everything the
post uses, e.g. data, images and a bibliography, goes in the same folder. The
file starts with a front matter block, followed by the text in Markdown:

```yaml
---
title: "Phonon results"
description: "One sentence shown in the list of posts."
author: "Your Name"
date: 2026-11-20
categories: [phonons]
draft: true
---
```

The title, description, date and categories are shown in the list of posts on
the front page, where the categories also work as filters. `draft: true` keeps
the post off the published blog while it is being written; it is still shown
by `pixi run preview`. Remove the line to publish the post.

The three example posts cover what most posts need:

- [*Writing a post*](https://tolborg-group.github.io/blog-template/posts/2026-11-01-writing-a-post/):
  Markdown, equations, citations, cross-references, callouts, tabs and margin
  notes.
- [*Python in a post*](https://tolborg-group.github.io/blog-template/posts/2026-11-05-python-figures/):
  figures, tables and numbers in the text that are computed from the data when
  the post is rendered.
- [*Interactive charts*](https://tolborg-group.github.io/blog-template/posts/2026-11-10-interactive-charts/):
  charts that the reader can hover over, zoom and pan, made with Altair.

Reading a post next to its source in `posts/` is the quickest way to learn the
syntax.

## Python in posts

A code block written as ```` ```{python} ```` is run when the post is
rendered, and whatever it prints or plots ends up in the post, as in a Jupyter
notebook. The block below is shown as it is written in a post, followed by its
output:

```{python}
#| echo: fenced
#| label: fig-lj
#| fig-cap: "The Lennard-Jones potential in reduced units."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

r = np.linspace(0.95, 3.0, 300)
V = 4 * (r**-12 - r**-6)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.plot(r, V, color="#0f766e")
ax.axhline(0, color="gray", linewidth=0.8, linestyle="--")
ax.set_xlabel(r"$r / \sigma$")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$V / \varepsilon$")
ax.set_ylim(-1.2, 1.5)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```

The lines starting with `#|` are *cell options*. Here, the label and caption
turn the plot into a numbered figure that the text can refer to as @fig-lj.
Other useful options are `echo: false`, which hides the code and keeps the
output, and `code-fold: true`, which hides the code behind a "Code" toggle, as
in the block below.

A post is a web page, so its figures can also be interactive. The chart below
is made with [Altair](https://altair-viz.github.io): hover over a curve to read
off values, click on the legend to highlight a gas, and scroll or drag to zoom
and pan.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

# Approximate Lennard-Jones parameters: epsilon in meV, sigma in Ångström.
gases = {"Ne": (3.1, 2.75), "Ar": (10.3, 3.40), "Kr": (14.1, 3.65), "Xe": (19.7, 3.98)}

r = np.linspace(2.5, 8.0, 300)
df = pd.concat(
    pd.DataFrame({
        "gas": gas,
        "r": r,
        "V": 4 * eps * ((sigma / r) ** 12 - (sigma / r) ** 6),
    })
    for gas, (eps, sigma) in gases.items()
)

highlight = alt.selection_point(fields=["gas"], bind="legend")
hover = alt.selection_point(fields=["r"], nearest=True, on="pointerover", empty=False)

base = alt.Chart(df).encode(
    x=alt.X("r:Q", title="Distance (Å)"),
    y=alt.Y("V:Q", title="Energy (meV)", scale=alt.Scale(domain=[-22, 10])),
    color=alt.Color("gas:N", title="Gas"),
)
lines = base.mark_line(clip=True).encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(highlight, alt.value(1), alt.value(0.15)),
).add_params(highlight)
points = base.mark_point(clip=True, filled=True, size=50).encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(hover, alt.value(1), alt.value(0)),
    tooltip=[
        # format="" works around a bug in Vega-Lite 6.4 that shows "undefined"
        # with nearest=True.
        alt.Tooltip("gas:N", title="Gas", format=""),
        alt.Tooltip("r:Q", title="r (Å)", format=".2f"),
        alt.Tooltip("V:Q", title="V (meV)", format=".2f"),
    ],
).add_params(hover)

(lines + points).properties(width="container", height=320).interactive()
```

The code runs in the Pixi environment of the blog, which has NumPy, pandas,
Matplotlib and Altair. A package that a post needs is added with `pixi add`,
see [Adding packages](pixi.qmd#adding-packages), and the updated `pixi.toml`
and `pixi.lock` are committed with the post.

The blog is set up with `freeze: auto`, which means that the code of a post is
only run again when its `index.qmd` changes. The results are stored in
`_freeze/`, which is committed together with the post. Old posts therefore keep
working when the code or data they used has moved on, and a post can show
results from data that is too large for the repository or from calculations
that only run on the cluster: GitHub only needs the stored results to publish
the blog.

::: {.callout-important}
Commit the post's folder in `_freeze/` together with the post. If the stored
results are missing, the post is run again when the blog is published, which
fails if the data is not in the repository.
:::

## Help from Claude

The template comes with the `/git:sync` skill from the
[group skills](../ai/skills.qmd), which commits, pulls and pushes the blog for
those who do not use git daily. If Claude Code is installed,

```bash
pixi run setup-claude
```

installs the group's plugins once, after which `pixi run sync` starts Claude
Code and runs the skill.
